title: scHelix: Asymmetric Dual-Stream Integration via Explicit Gene-Level Disentanglement

paper.title: scHelix : Asymmetric Dual-Stream Integration via Explicit Gene-Level Disentanglement
paper.abstract: Abstract. A critical challenge in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) integration is resolving the tension between eliminating batch effects and maintaining biological fidelity. While recent evidence indicates that batch effects manifest heterogeneously across genes, most existing methods process the transcriptome uniformly, frequently resulting in over-correction and loss of subtle biological signals. To address this, we present scHelix , a dataset-adaptive framework that fundamentally changes how features are processed by explicitly partitioning genes into domain-invariant Anchors and domain-sensitive Variants at the input level. scHelix utilizes a dual-stream sparse diffusion encoder equipped with stop-gradient graph caching to efficiently learn multi-scale structural representations. The core of our approach is a novel asymmetric Align-Refine-Fuse protocol: the unstable Variant stream is first aligned to the robust topology of the Anchor stream, followed by a conservative refinement phase where the Anchor stream absorbs denoised details via bounded residual gating. This “divide-and-conquer” architecture prevents shortcut learning and ensures robust batch removal without compromising the integrity of biological clusters. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that scHelix outperforms state-of-the-art methods.The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/scHelix-E175

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) integration is the cornerstone of constructing unified cell atlases, unlocking the potential to map dynamic trajectories across diverse populations ( Trapnell, 2015 ; Luecken et al., 2022 ) . However, it faces a fundamental trade-off: removing technical batch effects often comes at the cost of erasing subtle biological heterogeneity ( Leek et al., 2010 ; Haghverdi et al., 2018 ) . Aggressive correction methods tend to over-smooth data, blurring fine-grained cell states, while conservative approaches fail to align shared populations across domains ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) . This tension persists because most existing methods treat the transcriptome uniformly, processing the entire gene space (e.g., HVGs) as a monolithic feature vector ( Lopez et al., 2018 ; Korsunsky et al., 2019a ; Stuart et al., 2019 ) . This ignores a critical reality: batch effects are highly gene-specific ( Zhou et al., 2025a ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , genes governing core cellular programs—such as cell-cycle regulators (e.g., PCNA )—often maintain consistent distributions across platforms, providing a robust scaffold for cell identity. Conversely, context-sensitive genes—such as the interferon-stimulated gene ISG15 —carry genuine biological signals but are simultaneously confounded by technical artifacts. By forcing these conflicting signals into a single latent space, existing models often settle for a brittle compromise: either residual batch effects or loss of biological fidelity ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) . To address these challenges, we argue that integration methods must move beyond implicit latent space regularization to explicit feature-level disentanglement ( Lotfollahi et al., 2019 ; Piran et al., 2024 ) . Specifically, we answer three core questions: (1) Unsupervised Anchor Discovery : How can we identify a feature scaffold that is biologically discriminative yet technically stable, without relying on external annotations? (2) Structural Disentanglement : How do we prevent domain-sensitive noise from dominating the representation learning process (i.e., avoiding shortcut learning)? (3) Safe Interaction : How can we recover fine-grained details from noisy features without reintroducing batch artifacts into the stable topology? We propose scHelix , a "divide-and-conquer" framework that explicitly disentangles features at the input level. Instead of a uniform input, scHelix partitions genes into domain-invariant Anchors and domain-sensitive Variants using a dataset-adaptive discriminability-sensitivity criterion ( Section 3.2 ). This acts as a self-supervised feature selector , creating a hard information barrier: the Anchor stream serves as a stable "Teacher" to preserve topology, while the Variant stream acts as a "Student" tasked with denoising. Unlike MLP-based methods that treat cells as independent samples ( Lopez et al., 2018 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ) , scHelix employs a dual-stream sparse diffusion encoder to capture the non-linear manifold structure of the data ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Klicpera et al., 2019 ) . Crucially, we introduce a novel asymmetric Align-Refine-Fuse protocol. First, the unstable Variant stream aligns to the robust Anchor topology. Second, the Anchor stream conservatively absorbs denoised details via bounded residual gating. Finally, the streams are fused via a hyper-network. This serial, controlled interaction ensures robust batch removal without compromising the integrity of biological clusters. Our contributions are: • Explicit Disentanglement : A dataset-adaptive partition strategy that separates stable anchors from noisy variants, providing an interpretable biological scaffold. • Asymmetric Graph Architecture : A dual-stream design that leverages graph diffusion to learn multi-scale structural representations while strictly isolating noise sources. • Align-Refine-Fuse Protocol : A conservative interaction mechanism that balances topology preservation with detail recovery, preventing anchor contamination. • SOTA Performance : Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that scHelix achieves a superior trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

sections.heading: Batch correction and feature heterogeneity.
sections.text: Single-cell integration seeks to remove technical batch effects while preserving biological structure. Classical methods align datasets via cross-domain neighbor or anchor matching—e.g., MNN, Seurat, and Harmony ( Haghverdi et al., 2018 ; Korsunsky et al., 2019b ; Stuart et al., 2019 ) —while deep generative models such as scVI scale integration by learning batch-conditioned latent spaces ( Lopez et al., 2018 ) . However, most approaches treat the transcriptome as a uniform feature vector and apply global alignment pressure, implicitly assuming batch effects are globally distributed. Recent gene-level analyses challenge this assumption: the Group Technical Effect (GTE) metric reveals that batch shifts are strongly gene-dependent and often dominated by a small subset of highly batch-sensitive genes ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) , motivating feature-aware correction strategies.

sections.heading: Disentanglement, dual-stream architectures, and self-supervised alignment.
sections.text: Disentangled representation learning—via latent regularizers (scGen, biolord) ( Lotfollahi et al., 2019 ; Piran et al., 2024 ) or causal-inspired factorized blocks (CRADLE-VAE, FCR, SCBD) ( Baek et al., 2024 ; Makino et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2024 ) —aims to separate biological from nuisance variation, yet implicit enforcement can be difficult to audit and may still permit leakage. Dual encoders (e.g., BioBatchNet) ( Liu et al., 2025 ) provide explicit architectural separation, asymmetric self-supervised objectives (BYOL/SimSiam) ( Chen and He, 2021a ; Grill et al., 2020a ) offer stable teacher targets, and graph-based encoders (e.g., scGNN) ( Wang et al., 2021 ) capture single-cell topology. Our method builds on these ideas but makes disentanglement explicit at the input level via Anchor/Variant gene partitioning, coupled with a conservative Align–Refine–Fuse protocol that transfers denoised details while protecting the invariant scaffold.

sections.heading: 3.4. Align-Refine Interaction & HyperFusion
sections.text: Design principle ( Figure 2 (C)). Naive fusion can reintroduce domain artifacts into the clean Anchor scaffold. To prevent this, scHelix enforces a strict Align-Refine-Fuse protocol, designed to prevent noise leakage from the unstable Variant stream back to the stable Anchor topology. The process proceeds as follows: (i) align the Variant stream to the Anchor stream, (ii) conservatively refine the Anchor stream using denoised Variant details, and (iii) fuse via a gated mechanism. Asymmetric Variant–Anchor Alignment. We align the unstable Variant stream to the robust Anchor topology using a BYOL/SimSiam-style objective ( Grill et al., 2020b ; Chen and He, 2021b ) . We minimize the negative cosine similarity between the Variant stream’s prediction 𝐩 S \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{S}} and the Anchor stream’s target 𝐳 T \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{T}} : (6) ℒ align ≔ 2 − 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ⟨ 𝐩 S , 𝐳 T ⟩ ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}\coloneqq 2-2\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\langle\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{S}},\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{T}}\right\rangle\right]. Crucially, the stop-gradient on 𝐳 T \mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{T}} ensures the Anchor manifold acts as a fixed topological guide, preventing it from being pulled toward the noisy Student distribution (i.e., preventing model collapse). sections.heading: Task, datasets, baselines, and metrics.
sections.text: We study multi-domain scRNA-seq integration as representation learning under domain shift ( Gong et al., 2016 ) . We benchmark five public datasets; the main text reports three representative ones (Table 1 ), with the remaining two deferred to the Appendix (Table 5 ). Baselines include Harmony, scVI, INSCT, SCALEX, sysVI, SCEMENT, and scCobra ( Korsunsky et al., 2019a ; Lopez et al., 2018 ; Simon et al., 2021 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ; Hrovatin et al., 2025 ; Chockalingam et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ). All methods share the same QC/HVG pool and a unified training/evaluation pipeline (Appendix B – C ). Following scIB conventions ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) , all metrics are scaled/flipped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] (higher is better). We report the standard scIB Overall score (40/60 batch/bio weighting); detailed metric definitions are provided in Table 1 .

sections.heading: Benchmark results.
sections.text: Table 1 summarizes three representative datasets (full five-dataset results with mean ± \pm std over three seeds: Appendix Table 5 ). Across all three, scHelix achieves the best Overall score, surpassing the second-best baseline by an average of 1.05%. Gains are most pronounced in distinguishing subtle cell states. On the Pancreas dataset, Harmony and scVI tend to over-merge Ductal and Acinar populations ( Figure 5 , red circles) in pursuit of batch removal, whereas scHelix preserves these local neighborhoods while maintaining comparable batch integration scores. This structural preservation is underpinned by molecular fidelity: scHelix maintains sharp expression boundaries of lineage-specific markers (e.g., KRT19 for Ductal vs. PRSS1 for Acinar ( Muraro et al., 2016 ) ), avoiding the “expression smoothing” common in VAE-based baselines where marker specificity is diluted by the Gaussian latent prior. sections.heading: Over-correction & Runtime.
sections.text: We employ a rigorous over-correction stress test following scCobra ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . As shown in Figure 6 , scHelix achieves the lowest OC scores among deep baselines, indicating superior local-neighborhood preservation. This performance does not sacrifice efficiency: scHelix scales linearly with cell number, processing the 30k-cell Pancreas dataset in ∼ \sim 150 s with peak memory under 4 GB on a single A100 GPU—comparable to lightweight Harmony ( ∼ \sim 120 s ) but significantly faster than scVI ( ∼ \sim 600 s ) and scGPT ( > > 2000 s ).

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis.
sections.text: We vary key hyperparameters on Human Pancreas ( complexBatch ). scHelix exhibits high stability ( Figure 7 ), with the Overall score fluctuating negligibly ( Δ ≤ 0.0065 \Delta\leq 0.0065 ) across a broad range of settings, indicating that the default configuration is near-optimal and no precise tuning is required.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: We presented scHelix , a framework that resolves the integration trade-off by explicitly disentangling input genes into stable Anchors and batch-sensitive Variants. Through a conservative Align-Refine-Fuse protocol, scHelix achieves precise batch correction while preserving subtle biological signals. Extensive benchmarks confirm its superiority over state-of-the-art methods and foundation models, establishing it as a robust tool for high-fidelity cell atlas construction.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: First, the graph-based architecture incurs higher costs than linear methods, potentially requiring optimization for multi-million cell datasets. Second, our strategy relies on the existence of shared biological signals; extreme non-overlapping batch effects may hinder effective anchor discovery.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations.
sections.text: As an AI tool for science, scHelix warrants careful use: the “refined” expression values are computational imputations and must not substitute for experimentally validated clinical diagnoses. Users must also adhere to data privacy regulations when processing patient-derived transcriptomics to prevent re-identification risks.

sections.heading: Appendix A Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we provide rigorous theoretical justifications for the “divide-and-conquer” mechanisms in scHelix . We analyze the spectral properties of the dual-stream graph encoder (Section 3.3 ) and the stability guarantees of the asymmetric refinement protocol (Section 3.4 ).

sections.heading: A.1. Spectral Analysis of Multi-Scale Graph Diffusion
sections.text: We formally demonstrate that the encoder operations defined in Eq. ( 5 ) function as complementary spectral filters on the learned gene-gene graph. Specifically, we show that 𝐙 low \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{low}} extracts the global data manifold (Low-Pass), while 𝐙 high \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{high}} captures fine-grained local variations (High-Pass).

sections.heading: Setup: Graph Fourier Transform.
sections.text: Let 𝒢 \mathcal{G} be the learned gene-gene graph with row-normalized adjacency matrix 𝐏 ∈ ℝ G ∗ × G ∗ \mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{G_{*}\times G_{*}} . Let 𝐏 = 𝐔 ​ 𝚲 ​ 𝐔 − 1 \mathbf{P}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^{-1} be its eigendecomposition, where 𝚲 = diag ​ ( λ 1 , … , λ G ∗ ) \mathbf{\Lambda}=\text{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{G_{*}}) contains eigenvalues ordered by magnitude 1 = λ 1 ≥ | λ 2 | ≥ ⋯ ≥ | λ G ∗ | ≥ 0 1=\lambda_{1}\geq|\lambda_{2}|\geq\dots\geq|\lambda_{G_{*}}|\geq 0 . The eigenvectors 𝐔 \mathbf{U} form the graph spectral basis. Any feature signal 𝐱 \mathbf{x} can be represented as 𝐱 = ∑ i c i ​ 𝐮 i \mathbf{x}=\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i} . Note that during the forward pass, the graph topology is fixed (via sg ⁡ ( 𝐏 ) \operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{P}) ), acting as a linear operator.

sections.heading: Theorem 1 (Complementary Spectral Filtering).
sections.text: The multi-scale features in Eq. ( 5 ) modulate the spectral coefficients c i c_{i} via the following transfer functions h ⁡ ( λ ) h(\lambda) : (11) 𝐙 low : \displaystyle\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{low}}:\quad h low ​ ( λ ) = λ k \displaystyle h_{\mathrm{low}}(\lambda)=\lambda^{k} (12) 𝐙 high : \displaystyle\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{high}}:\quad h high ​ ( λ ) = ξ 1 ​ ( 1 − λ k ) + ξ 2 ​ ( 1 − λ m ) \displaystyle h_{\mathrm{high}}(\lambda)=\xi_{1}(1-\lambda^{k})+\xi_{2}(1-\lambda^{m})

sections.heading: Proof.
sections.text: 1. Low-Pass (Global Structure): The low-frequency term is defined as 𝐙 low = 𝐗𝐏 k \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{low}}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{P}^{k} . Applying this operator to a basis vector 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} : (13) 𝐏 k ​ 𝐮 i = λ i k ​ 𝐮 i . \mathbf{P}^{k}\mathbf{u}_{i}=\lambda_{i}^{k}\mathbf{u}_{i}. The transfer function is h low ​ ( λ i ) = λ i k h_{\mathrm{low}}(\lambda_{i})=\lambda_{i}^{k} . Since | λ i | ≤ 1 |\lambda_{i}|\leq 1 , as the diffusion scale k k increases, high-frequency components (where | λ i | < 1 |\lambda_{i}|<1 ) decay exponentially ( λ i k → 0 \lambda_{i}^{k}\to 0 ). The DC component ( λ 1 = 1 \lambda_{1}=1 ) is preserved ( 1 k = 1 1^{k}=1 ). Thus, 𝐙 low \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{low}} effectively smooths out local noise and retains the global topological structure. 2. Substituting 𝐙 low = 𝐗𝐏 k \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{low}}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{P}^{k} , we have: (15) 𝐙 high = 𝐗 ⁡ [ ξ 1 ​ ( 𝐈 − 𝐏 k ) + ξ 2 ​ ( 𝐈 − 𝐏 m ) ] . \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{high}}=\mathbf{X}\bigl[\xi_{1}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}^{k})+\xi_{2}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}^{m})\bigr]. Global background is suppressed. • High Frequencies ( λ i → 0 \lambda_{i}\to 0 ): h high ​ ( λ i ) → ξ 1 ​ ( 1 ) + ξ 2 ​ ( 1 ) = ξ 1 + ξ 2 h_{\mathrm{high}}(\lambda_{i})\to\xi_{1}(1)+\xi_{2}(1)=\xi_{1}+\xi_{2} . Local signals are preserved/amplified. This proves that 𝐙 high \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{high}} acts as a high-pass filter, complementing the smoothing effect of the low-pass stream.

sections.heading: Intuitive Interpretation.
sections.text: Analogous to image processing, the multi-scale graph diffusion acts as a composite filter bank. The low-pass component ( 𝐙 low \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{low}} ) functions like a Gaussian blur, smoothing out stochastic gene expression noise to reveal the underlying cellular manifold (topology). The high-pass component ( 𝐙 high \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{high}} ), conversely, acts like an unsharp mask, highlighting sharp local transitions—such as the specific expression of marker genes that define boundaries between subtle subtypes. By explicitly separating these frequency bands, scHelix avoids the common pitfall of “oversmoothing” where fine-grained biological details are lost during batch correction.

sections.heading: A.2. Stability Analysis of Asymmetric Interaction
sections.text: We analyze the stability of the Align-Refine protocol. A key concern in integration is whether the noisy Variant stream (which may contain severe batch effects) can corrupt the stable Anchor stream during interaction. We prove that the Anchor stream is theoretically protected.

sections.heading: Proposition 2 (Boundedness and Continuity).
sections.text: Let 𝐇 i inv \mathbf{H}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}} be the stable anchor embedding. The refinement update 𝐇 ~ i inv = 𝐇 i inv + 𝜶 i ⊙ Δ ​ 𝐡 i \tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}}=\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}}+\bm{\alpha}_{i}\odot\Delta\mathbf{h}_{i} (Eq. ( 7 )) satisfies two stability properties: (1) Global Boundedness: The update magnitude is strictly capped by α max \alpha_{\max} , independent of the Variant input 𝐡 i var \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\mathrm{var}} . (2) Lipschitz Continuity: The update function is Lipschitz continuous with respect to 𝐇 i var \mathbf{H}_{i}^{\mathrm{var}} , ensuring smooth gradient flow.

Since the normalized term ( 𝐯 − μ ) / σ (\mathbf{v}-\mu)/\sigma has unit variance, its Euclidean norm is exactly d \sqrt{d} . Thus, ‖ LN ⁡ ( 𝐯 ) ‖ 2 ≤ d ​ ‖ 𝜸 ‖ ∞ + ‖ 𝜷 ‖ 2 ≕ C LN \|\LN(\mathbf{v})\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\,\|\bm{\gamma}\|_{\infty}+\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}\eqqcolon C_{\LN} . Combined with the sigmoid gate ‖ 𝜶 i ‖ ∞ ≤ α max \|\bm{\alpha}_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq\alpha_{\max} , the total perturbation is bounded: (17) ‖ 𝐇 ~ i inv − 𝐇 i inv ‖ 2 = ‖ 𝜶 i ⊙ Δ ​ 𝐡 i ‖ 2 ≤ α max ​ C LN . \|\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}}-\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}}\|_{2}=\|\bm{\alpha}_{i}\odot\Delta\mathbf{h}_{i}\|_{2}\leq\alpha_{\max}C_{\LN}. This bound R = α max ​ C LN R=\alpha_{\max}C_{\LN} holds regardless of the magnitude of 𝐡 i var \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\mathrm{var}} (e.g., even under severe batch outliers). 2. Lipschitz Continuity (Smoothness). The functions composing the update—Sigmoid, LayerNorm, and Softmax (in Attention)—are all Lipschitz continuous and differentiable almost everywhere. This implies there exists a constant L L such that: (18) ‖ Δ ​ 𝐡 ~ i inv ​ ( 𝐱 ) − Δ ​ 𝐡 ~ i inv ​ ( 𝐲 ) ‖ 2 ≤ L ​ ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐲 ‖ 2 \|\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbf{x})-\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{i}^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbf{y})\|_{2}\leq L\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2} for any two Variant inputs 𝐱 , 𝐲 \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} . Consequently, small perturbations or noise in the Variant stream result in proportionally small changes in the Anchor update, preventing chaotic behavior or gradient explosion during fusion.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: The Anchor stream is doubly protected: it is mathematically confined to a safe ϵ \epsilon -ball around the stable manifold (Boundedness), and its deformation within that ball is smooth and controlled (Continuity).

sections.heading: B.1. Shared preprocessing: QC, normalization, and HVG pool
sections.text: We follow a standard Scanpy-style pipeline for all datasets and all methods. We apply the same quality-control (QC) filters across benchmarks: (i) remove cells with fewer than 200 detected genes, (ii) remove genes expressed in fewer than 3 cells, and (iii) remove cells with mitochondrial gene percentage exceeding 5%. After QC, we normalize each cell to a library size of 10,000 and apply log ⁡ ( 1 + x ) \log(1+x) . We then select G sel = 2000 G_{\mathrm{sel}}=2000 highly variable genes (HVGs) using batch-aware HVG selection. For fair comparison, all methods share the same QC filters and the same HVG pool.

sections.heading: B.2. Two synchronized data views (fairness & method compliance)
sections.text: To respect method-specific input assumptions without giving any method extra information, we maintain two synchronized views after QC, always restricted to the same HVG pool when a method requires it: • Raw counts view : the integer count matrix (after QC). Used by count-based generative models (e.g., scVI-style pipelines). • Log-normalized view : library-size normalized to 10,000, then log ⁡ ( 1 + x ) \log(1+x) . Used by PCA/distance-based methods (e.g., Harmony) and preprocessing-dependent components.

sections.heading: B.3. MixUp-style augmentation (training only)
sections.text: During training, we optionally apply a k mix k_{\mathrm{mix}} -nearest-neighbor MixUp strategy (e.g., k mix = 300 k_{\mathrm{mix}}=300 ). For each cell 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} , we sample a neighbor 𝐱 j \mathbf{x}_{j} and construct an augmented sample: (19) 𝐱 aug ≔ α ​ 𝐱 i + ( 1 − α ) ​ 𝐱 j , α ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) . \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{aug}}\coloneqq\alpha\,\mathbf{x}_{i}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_{j},\qquad\alpha\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1). We do not use augmentation in validation/evaluation.

sections.heading: C.1. Optimization details
sections.text: We optimize parameters using AdamW and apply gradient clipping for stability. For the learnable sparse feature graphs, cached graph topologies and cached multi-scale diffusion powers are rebuilt periodically every T T steps to reduce overhead.

sections.heading: C.2. Unified evaluation representation: PCA-64 as a robust cap
sections.text: Many scIB-style metrics ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) (e.g., ASW, GC, and Leiden-based ARI / NMI \mathrm{ARI}/\mathrm{NMI} ) are computed from a kNN graph in an embedding space. Because methods output embeddings with different dimensionalities, we apply a PCA-64 evaluation cap to prevent metric variance caused purely by representation dimension: • If a method outputs an embedding with dimension d > 64 d>64 , we project it to 64 dimensions via PCA before computing kNN/Leiden/metrics. • If a method outputs d ≤ 64 d\leq 64 , we evaluate on its native embedding (no artificial up-projection).

sections.heading: Why 64?
sections.text: scIB-style pipelines commonly use a moderate PCA dimensionality (often ∼ 50 {\sim}50 PCs) to build neighbor graphs. We use 64 as a slightly higher but still moderate, stable setting for kNN-based metrics.

sections.heading: C.3. Raw baseline used in OC normalization
sections.text: For normalized over-correction (OC) in Appendix G , the Raw baseline refers to the uncorrected representation computed from the log-normalized HVG expression (Appendix B.2 ): • HD Raw space (pre-UMAP) : log-normalized HVGs → \rightarrow (Scanpy/scIB-style scaling if applicable) → \rightarrow PCA-64 . • UMAP Raw space : 2D UMAP computed from the above Raw PCA-64 representation.

sections.heading: C.4. Clustering protocol for ARI best / NMI best \mathrm{ARI}_{\mathrm{best}}/\mathrm{NMI}_{\mathrm{best}}
sections.text: Following the scIB benchmarking protocol ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) , we compute a kNN graph on the evaluation representation and run Leiden clustering over a fixed resolution grid. We report ARI best \mathrm{ARI}_{\mathrm{best}} / NMI best \mathrm{NMI}_{\mathrm{best}} using the best result over the sweep.

sections.heading: C.5. Metric definitions (scIB-style; scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] when applicable)
sections.text: All metrics are computed on the unified evaluation representation described in Appendix C.2 . When a metric is naturally defined on [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , we linearly rescale it to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] for consistent aggregation. All metric definitions and the overall aggregation scheme follow the scIB benchmark ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: Hardware.
sections.text: All experiments are run on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU (11 GB).

sections.heading: Why the method scales.
sections.text: The method avoids dense G × G G\times G feature interactions by learning sparse feature graphs (Top- k k per gene). Graph topology is rebuilt periodically and reused via stop-gradient caching, and multi-scale diffusion powers are cached for reuse.

sections.heading: Gene-level graphs, not cell-level graphs.
sections.text: A key design choice is that the learnable sparse graphs in scHelix are feature-level (gene–gene) adjacency matrices of size G ∗ × G ∗ G_{*}\times G_{*} (where G ∗ ≤ G sel = 2,000 G_{*}\leq G_{\mathrm{sel}}=2{,}000 ), not cell-level ( N × N N\times N ) graphs. We emphasize this distinction because cell-level graph construction would incur 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}) cost, which is prohibitive for large atlases ( N > 10 5 N>10^{5} ). In contrast, the adjacency construction cost in scHelix is 𝒪 ⁡ ( G ∗ 2 ⋅ d a ) \mathcal{O}(G_{*}^{2}\cdot d_{a}) per rebuild (with d a d_{a} being the attention dimension), which is negligible: for G ∗ ≈ 1,000 G_{*}\approx 1{,}000 and d a = 64 d_{a}=64 , a single rebuild involves ∼ 6.4 × 10 7 {\sim}\!6.4\times 10^{7} operations—orders of magnitude smaller than a single forward pass over the data. Cell-level computation involves only the sparse matrix product 𝐗 ∗ ∈ ℝ N × G ∗ \mathbf{X}_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times G_{*}} multiplied by 𝐏 ∗ ∈ ℝ G ∗ × G ∗ \mathbf{P}_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{G_{*}\times G_{*}} , scaling as 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ⋅ G ∗ ⋅ k ) \mathcal{O}(N\cdot G_{*}\cdot k) where k k is the Top- k k sparsity level— linear in the number of cells N N . The graph 𝐏 ∗ \mathbf{P}_{*} is a global gene–gene relation graph shared across all cells; it is not constructed per mini-batch but rebuilt periodically (every T T steps) and cached. Combined with stop-gradient caching of multi-hop powers, this ensures that scHelix scales to datasets with hundreds of thousands of cells on a single GPU (Table 9 ), and the architecture itself does not impose a fundamental barrier to million-cell datasets—scaling to such regimes would primarily require standard engineering optimizations (e.g., mini-batch sampling) rather than architectural changes. sections.text: Fully differentiable sparse graph learning with multi-hop powers is computationally prohibitive for G ∼ 10 3 G\sim 10^{3} and tends to introduce gradient instability due to discrete top- k k selection and matrix power compositions. Our piecewise-constant topology strategy balances (i) learnability (via the 1-hop path), (ii) stability (stop-gradient for multi-hop), and (iii) efficiency (reuse cached powers).

A critical challenge in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) integration is resolving the tension between eliminating batch effects and maintaining biological fidelity. While recent evidence indicates that batch effects manifest heterogeneously across genes, most existing methods process the transcriptome uniformly, frequently resulting in over-correction and loss of subtle biological signals. To address this, we present scHelix , a dataset-adaptive framework that fundamentally changes how features are processed by explicitly partitioning genes into domain-invariant Anchors and domain-sensitive Variants at the input level. scHelix utilizes a dual-stream sparse diffusion encoder equipped with stop-gradient graph caching to efficiently learn multi-scale structural representations. The core of our approach is a novel asymmetric Align-Refine-Fuse protocol: the unstable Variant stream is first aligned to the robust topology of the Anchor stream, followed by a conservative refinement phase where the Anchor stream absorbs denoised details via bounded residual gating. This “divide-and-conquer” architecture prevents shortcut learning and ensures robust batch removal without compromising the integrity of biological clusters. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that scHelix outperforms state-of-the-art methods.The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/scHelix-E175 Keywords: Single-cell integration; disentangled representation learning; graph neural networks; batch effect correction; self-supervised learning 1. Anchor Genes (AG) serve as a stable scaffold, while Variant Genes (VG) are prone to domain noise. (B) The Strategy : scHelix partitions genes into invariant ( G inv G_{\text{inv}} ) and variant ( G var G_{\text{var}} ) streams. The Anchor Backbone (Teacher) guides the Variant Refiner (Student) to align and denoise, preserving topology in the fused representation ( H fused H_{\text{fused}} ). Conceptual diagram showing the scHelix motivation: panel A illustrates gene-specific batch effects with Anchor Genes being stable and Variant Genes being noisy across domains; panel B shows the dual-stream strategy where an invariant Anchor backbone guides a Variant Refiner to produce a fused representation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) integration is the cornerstone of constructing unified cell atlases, unlocking the potential to map dynamic trajectories across diverse populations ( Trapnell, 2015 ; Luecken et al., 2022 ) . However, it faces a fundamental trade-off: removing technical batch effects often comes at the cost of erasing subtle biological heterogeneity ( Leek et al., 2010 ; Haghverdi et al., 2018 ) . Aggressive correction methods tend to over-smooth data, blurring fine-grained cell states, while conservative approaches fail to align shared populations across domains ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) . This tension persists because most existing methods treat the transcriptome uniformly, processing the entire gene space (e.g., HVGs) as a monolithic feature vector ( Lopez et al., 2018 ; Korsunsky et al., 2019a ; Stuart et al., 2019 ) . This ignores a critical reality: batch effects are highly gene-specific ( Zhou et al., 2025a ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 , genes governing core cellular programs—such as cell-cycle regulators (e.g., PCNA )—often maintain consistent distributions across platforms, providing a robust scaffold for cell identity. Conversely, context-sensitive genes—such as the interferon-stimulated gene ISG15 —carry genuine biological signals but are simultaneously confounded by technical artifacts. By forcing these conflicting signals into a single latent space, existing models often settle for a brittle compromise: either residual batch effects or loss of biological fidelity ( Luecken et al., 2022 ) . To address these challenges, we argue that integration methods must move beyond implicit latent space regularization to explicit feature-level disentanglement ( Lotfollahi et al., 2019 ; Piran et al., 2024 ) . Specifically, we answer three core questions: (1) Unsupervised Anchor Discovery : How can we identify a feature scaffold that is biologically discriminative yet technically stable, without relying on external annotations? (2) Structural Disentanglement : How do we prevent domain-sensitive noise from dominating the representation learning process (i.e., avoiding shortcut learning)? (3) Safe Interaction : How can we recover fine-grained details from noisy features without reintroducing batch artifacts into the stable topology? We propose scHelix , a "divide-and-conquer" framework that explicitly disentangles features at the input level. Instead of a uniform input, scHelix partitions genes into domain-invariant Anchors and domain-sensitive Variants using a dataset-adaptive discriminability-sensitivity criterion ( Section 3.2 ). This acts as a self-supervised feature selector , creating a hard information barrier: the Anchor stream serves as a stable "Teacher" to preserve topology, while the Variant stream acts as a "Student" tasked with denoising. Unlike MLP-based methods that treat cells as independent samples ( Lopez et al., 2018 ; Xiong et al., 2022 ) , scHelix employs a dual-stream sparse diffusion encoder to capture the non-linear manifold structure of the data ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Klicpera et al., 2019 ) . Crucially, we introduce a novel asymmetric Align-Refine-Fuse protocol. First, the unstable Variant stream aligns to the robust Anchor topology. Second, the Anchor stream conservatively absorbs denoised details via bounded residual gating. Finally, the streams are fused via a hyper-network. This serial, controlled interaction ensures robust batch removal without compromising the integrity of biological clusters. Our contributions are: • Explicit Disentanglement : A dataset-adaptive partition strategy that separates stable anchors from noisy variants, providing an interpretable biological scaffold. • Asymmetric Graph Architecture : A dual-stream design that leverages graph diffusion to learn multi-scale structural representations while strictly isolating noise sources. • Align-Refine-Fuse Protocol : A conservative interaction mechanism that balances topology preservation with detail recovery, preventing anchor contamination. • SOTA Performance : Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that scHelix achieves a superior trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation compared to state-of-the-art baselines. 2. Related Work Batch correction and feature heterogeneity. Single-cell integration seeks to remove technical batch effects while preserving biological structure. Classical methods align datasets via cross-domain neighbor or anchor matching—e.g., MNN, Seurat, and Harmony ( Haghverdi et al., 2018 ; Korsunsky et al., 2019b ; Stuart et al., 2019 ) —while deep generative models such as scVI scale integration by learning batch-conditioned latent spaces ( Lopez et al., 2018 ) . However, most approaches treat the transcriptome as a uniform feature vector and apply global alignment pressure, implicitly assuming batch effects are globally distributed. Recent gene-level analyses challenge this assumption: the Group Technical Effect (GTE) metric reveals that batch shifts are strongly gene-dependent and often dominated by a small subset of highly batch-sensitive genes ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) , motivating feature-aware correction strategies. Disentanglement, dual-stream architectures, and self-supervised alignment. Disentangled representation learning—via latent regularizers (scGen, biolord) ( Lotfollahi et al., 2019 ; Piran et al., 2024 ) or causal-inspired factorized blocks (CRADLE-VAE, FCR, SCBD) ( Baek et al., 2024 ; Makino et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2024 ) —aims to separate biological from nuisance variation, yet implicit enforcement can be difficult to audit and may still permit leakage. Dual encoders (e.g., BioBatchNet) ( Liu et al., 2025 ) provide explicit architectural separation, asymmetric self-supervised objectives (BYOL/SimSiam) ( Chen and He, 2021a ; Grill et al., 2020a ) offer stable teacher targets, and graph-based encoders (e.g., scGNN) ( Wang et al., 2021 ) capture single-cell topology. Our method builds on these ideas but makes disentanglement explicit at the input level via Anchor/Variant gene partitioning, coupled with a conservative Align–Refine–Fuse protocol that transfers denoised details while protecting the invariant scaffold. 3.
